newsitem.title: UK: Clarke wins cautious welcome for pre-poll budget.
newsitem.headline: Clarke wins cautious welcome for pre-poll budget.

text.p: Finance minister Kenneth Clarke on Tuesday unveiled a pre-election budget carefully crafted to woo Britain's wavering voters with a modest cut in basic income tax and extra spending on schools, hospitals and the police.
But Clarke raised a number of indirect taxes and scrapped a number of tax breaks, resulting in a relatively tight overall budget meant to head off a damaging rise in interest rates.

"This budget secures a prosperous future for all sections of our people and their families. It is a budget not just for today but for tomorrow. This is a sensible budget for growing prosperity," he said.

Clarke described the budget as "responsible" and "virtuous" and said it would pave the way for the ruling Conservatives to come from behind in the opinion polls and win a fifth consecutive term in office at an election, due by May 22.
"Never forget, good economics is good politics...It is a budget that this government will build upon again in twelve months' time," he said.
Clarke cut overall taxes by two billion pounds ($3.34 billion) but offset it by reducing public spending by the same amount.

Economists estimated the overall net "giveaway" at a modest 735 million pounds ($1.2 billion) -- smaller than some Conservatives wanted but true to Clarke's promise to put the health of the economy first.
"A fiscal stimulus to the economy at this stage could be just as damaging as letting go of monetary policy. So, in setting my budget, I have struck a careful balance," he said.

Financial markets gave a collective shrug, while opposition politicians predictably condemned the budget, saying it relied too heavily on projected savings from a crackdown on fraud and tax avoidance and disguised a big rise in local council tax.
"One thing we now know for certain is that taxes will be higher at the next election than the last," Tony Blair, leader of the main opposition Labour party, told parliament.

In a naked pitch to the voters, Clarke said his tax plans -- including rises in thresholds that mean one in four taxpayers is now paying just the 20 percent starting rate -- would make the average family 370 pounds better off next year after inflation.

Blair, in a battle of figures sure to be repeated many times in the election campaign, countered that the average British taxpayer now paid 2,120 pounds more in tax than at the time of the last election in 1992.

The centrepiece of the budget, which was overshadowed by an unprecedented leak of the budget to the Daily Mirror newspaper on Monday night, was a widely trailed cut in the basic rate of income tax from 24 percent to 23 percent -- a 60-year low.
Clarke said he expected economic growth to accelerate to 3.5 percent in 1997, from 2.5 percent this year, keeping Britain as the fastest-growing major economy in Europe.
He said: "These are the best circumstances we have faced for a generation. This is a Rolls Royce recovery -- built to last."
John Redwood, the right-winger who challenged Prime Minister John Major for the Conservative leadership last year, said Clarke had been right to focus on keeping the economy humming.

But he could not disguise his disappointment that tax and spending cuts had not been deeper: "It is not an election-winning budget in the sense that it does not give away an awful lot of money that we can't afford to give away."

As Clarke spoke, a high-level investigation was under way into the leak of a sheaf of budget papers to the Daily Mirror. Prime Minister John Major's office confirmed late on Tuesday that the police has been called in to investigate the incident.
The leak, the worst in half a century, acutely embarrassed the government, which is struggling to shake off the perception that it is losing its touch after 17-1/2 years in power. ($1=.5990 Pound)
